'''Andrew Munro''', M.A., (6 July 1869 – 1 July 1935) was a [[Scottish culture|Scottish]] lecturer in mathematics, Vice President, Bursar, Steward and Senior Fellow of [[Queens' College, Cambridge]] for 45 years from 1893 to 1935.  The Munro scholarships and studentships at Queens' College, Cambridge are named in his honour.

==Early life==
Andrew Munro was born 6 July 1869, in Rosskeen, [[Ross and Cromarty]], [[Scotland]], the son of Andrew Munro and Margaret Small of [[Invergordon]] in Ross and Cromarty.<ref name="The Scotsman Article">{{cite news|title=The Late Mr. Andrew Munro, of Cambridge|newspaper=The Scotsman |location=Edinburgh, Scotland|date=4 July 1935}}</ref> His father was a banker, mill owner and farmer,<ref name="Freedom of the City Papers">{{cite document|title=London, England, Freedom of the City Papers, 1681- 1925|publisher=Ancestry.com|location=Salt Lake City, UT, USA |date=16 November 1923|quote=Papers for Andrew's brother, William Ross Munro}}</ref> who also served as [[Chief Magistrate]] for [[Invergordon]] and [[Justice of the Peace]] for Ross and Cromarty.<ref name="Obituary for Andrew Munro Sr.">{{cite news|title=Article on the Death of Andrew Munro|newspaper=The Scotsman|location=Edinburgh, Scotland|date=21 May 1888|quote=Mr. Munro was Chief Magistrate for the town, a Justice of Peace for the county, and also held other offices.}}</ref> The Munros were members of the [[Clan Munro]].  His mother was the daughter of John Small (1797–1847), under Librarian of the [[University of Edinburgh]], and the sister of [[John Small (librarian)|John Small (1828–1886)]], who succeeded his father as under Librarian and later was appointed Librarian.  Munro's mother and family were members of the Smalls of [[Dirnanean House|Dirnanean]], Perthshire, Scotland.

==Academics==
Munro initially attended [[Aberdeen University]], Scotland, later transferring to Cambridge.<ref name="The Scotsman Article" /> He won a foundation scholarship to [[Queens' College, Cambridge]] in 1890, and two years later was designated as the fourth [[Wrangler (University of Cambridge)|Wrangler]].<ref name="The Scotsman Article" />

In 1892, Munro received his Bachelor of Arts degree, followed by a [[Masters of Arts]] degree in 1896.<ref name="Oxford and Cambridge Yearbook">{{cite book|title=The Oxford and Cambridge Yearbook|year=1904}}</ref> In 1893, he was elected a [[Fellow]] at Queens' College, Cambridge.<ref name="The Scotsman Article" /> For the next 20 years he served as a lecturer, director of studies, and supervisor in mathematics at the college.<ref name="The Scotsman Article" />

In 1913, Munro became [[Bursar]] of Queens' College, Cambridge.<ref name="The Scotsman Article" /> In this role, Munro advised the college to dispose of most of its farmland after [[World War I]] and invest in government stocks, which significantly increased the college's [[financial endowment|endowments]].<ref name="The Scotsman Article" /><ref name="The Times Obituary" />

==Legacy==
Andrew Munro died on 1 July 1935 at Dormy House Hotel in [[Sheringham]], Norfolk, England.<ref name="UK Probate">{{cite document|title=England and Wales, National Probate Calendar, 1858 – 1966|publisher=Ancestry.com |location=Salt Lake City, UT, USA}}</ref> He was buried in St. Giles Cemetery in Cambridge, now referred to as [[Ascension Parish Burial Ground, Cambridge|Parish of the Ascension Burial Ground]], on 4 July 1935.<ref name="The Times Obituary">{{cite news|title=Obituary, Mr. Andrew Munro, Queens' College, Cambridge|newspaper=The Times|location= London, UK|date=3 July 1935}}</ref>

A portion of Munro's estate, upwards of £26,000, was left to Queens' College, Cambridge to fund scholarships in mathematics and [[physics]].<ref name="Queens' College Endowments">{{cite web|title=British History Online: Queens' College Endowments|url=http://www.british-history.ac.uk/report.aspx?compid=66650|publisher=University of London & History of Parliament Trust|year=2012}}</ref> These scholarships and studentships are named in Munro's honour.

The Munro Room at Queens' College, Cambridge which faces both [[Queens' College, Cambridge#Old Court|Old Court]] and [[Queens' College, Cambridge#Walnut Tree Court|Walnut Tree Court]], is named for Munro.  A portrait of Munro, painted by [[Arthur Trevor Haddon]], appropriately hangs in the room.
